title: The Railway Children

subtitle.text: The children were not "railway children" at the beginning.
In fact, they never thought about the railway at all!
They were ordinary children who lived in a brick house with their mother and father in London.
Roberta was the oldest, and she was always called Bobbie.
Next was Peter—he was ten years old and wanted to be a train engineer when he grew up.
The youngest was Phyllis.
She was eight years old and tried to be good all the time.
These three lucky children had everything they needed— nice clothes, a warm house, and lots of toys.
The children's mother was almost always at home and often played with the children or read to them.
Their father was rarely angry or unjust and was always ready to play a game.
They were all very happy.
But the children did not know how lucky they were until one evening.
That was when a knock came at their front door.
From this moment on, their lives were changed forever.
Peter had a birthday—his tenth.
Father was at work.
But his sisters, Bobbie and Phyllis, and his mother all gave him presents in the morning.
One of these presents was a model engine, and Peter was overjoyed.
Peter's joy lasted for three days until the engine suddenly went bang
! The engine was
broken. Peter was very
unhappy. His sisters said he had cried, but Peter insisted his eyes were red from a
cold. When Father came home that evening, Peter told him the story of the broken
engine. Father looked at the toy engine
carefully. "Hmm," said Father. The children waited
impatiently. "Is there any hope?" asked
Peter. "Yes, it can be fixed with some tools—but not tonight," said Father
cheerfully. "Let's wait till Saturday and you can all help me fix
it." "Can girls help to fix engines?" Peter asked
doubtfully. "Of course! Girls are just as clever as boys, and don't you forget it!" Father
said. "How would you like to be an engine driver,
Phyllis?" "No, my face would always be dirty," said
Phyllis. "I would just love it," said
Bobbie. "Can I be an engine driver when I grow up,
Father?" "Yes, we'll help you!" Father
replied. Suddenly there was a knock at the
door. "Who's that?" said
Father. Mother came in and said that two gentlemen wanted to see
Father. "They're in the next room," she
added. "I hope they leave soon because it's nearly the children's
bedtime." But the visitors stayed until
late. Mother told the children a story about a princess with green
eyes. It was difficult for the children to listen because voices came from the next room.
Father's voice sounded louder than usual.
He even sounded angry.
Ruth, the maid, came in.
"He wants you to go in, ma'am," she said to Mother.
"I think he's had bad news.
Be ready for the worst."
So Mother went into the next room, and there was more talking.
Later Mother came back, and her face was pale.
"It's bedtime," she said. "Ruth will put you to bed."
"But you promised we could stay up with Father!" said Phyllis.
"Father had to leave—on business," said Mother.
The children kissed her and went to bed. Bobbie lingered.
She hugged Mother and whispered, "It wasn't bad news, was it, Mommy?
Did someone . . . die?"
"Nobody died, no," said Mother, and she almost seemed to push Bobbie away.
When the children woke up the next morning, Mother was gone.
"I think something awful has happened," said Peter during breakfast.
"I asked Ruth, and she said we'll find out soon."
"You should have waited to ask Mother!" Bobbie said angrily.
It was seven o'clock in the evening when Mother came home.
She looked worn-out.
After she rested and had a cup of tea, she said,
"My darlings, I want to tell you something.
Those men did bring very bad news last night.
Father won't be here for some time.
I am very worried, and I want you to help me.
You can help me by being good and not quarreling."
The children wondered why Father had to leave.
What could have happened?
The children were gathered around Mother.
They had found out Father had to leave suddenly on business.
But why was Mother so upset?
And when would Father be back?
"Please don't ask me any questions about this," Mother said.
"I'm sorry, but I can't answer them.
And please don't ask anyone else either."
Peter looked down, his cheeks flushed.
"You'll promise, won't you?" said Mother.
"I asked Ruth," said Peter. "I'm very sorry."
"What did she say?" Mother asked.
"She said we would find out soon."
"You don't need to know anything," said Mother, "because it's about business.
Do you understand business?"
"No," answered Bobbie.
"Is it something to do with the government?"
Father worked for the government.
"Yes," said Mother.
"And don't you worry, everything will be fine."
"Don't you worry either, Mother!" said Phyllis.
"We'll be as good as gold!"
Mother sighed and kissed them, and they went to bed.
Over the next few weeks, Mother was often out.
Aunt Emma came to visit.
Aunt Emma was much older than Mother.
She was always busy sewing clothes and wasn't much fun.
The children preferred the company of the servants, who were more amusing.
If the cook was in a good mood, she would sing silly songs.
One day Peter made a booby trap.
He balanced a pail of flour over the bathroom door.
When Ruth moved the door, flour fell on her head.
"You'll be in trouble!" Ruth said furiously.
"If you don't behave yourself, you'll end up where your precious father's gone!"
Peter wondered what Ruth was talking about.
One morning Mother came down to breakfast. She smiled.
"Now, my darlings," she said.
"We're going to leave this house, and go and live in the country.
We'll move into a little white house.
I know you'll love it."
A busy week followed, with everyone packing up things in boxes.
They packed crockery and carpets, saucepans and candlesticks.
"Are you going to take this, Mother?" Bobbie asked.
She pointed to a beautiful cabinet of wood and brass.
"We can't take everything!" Mother exclaimed.
"But we seem to be taking all the ugly things," said Bobbie.
"We're taking all the useful things," said Mother.
"We don't have as much money now, Bobbie."
The next day the children said good-bye to their house.
They went with Mother to the train station.
Aunt Emma waved good-bye from the platform.
The children were glad they wouldn't see her again!
They were taking the train to their new home.
At first the children enjoyed looking out the train window.
But as dusk came, they grew sleepier and sleepier.
Later Mother gently woke them and said, "We're here!"
Soon Bobbie, Phyllis, and Peter stood shivering with their mother on the windy platform.
The train, puffing steam, left the station.
The children watched it go.
It was the first train they watched on the railway.
They didn't know it yet, but the railway would soon become very special to them.
"Come on," said Mother. "We have to walk.
There aren't any taxis here."
A cart carried their luggage.
The children and Mother walked behind the cart.
The evening was dark and cold and the road was muddy.
Finally Mother spoke again.
"There's the house," she said.
The children and Mother stared at the dark house.
"I wonder why the windows are closed.
I asked Mrs. Viney to open them," Mother said.
"Who's she?" asked Bobbie.
"The woman I asked to clean and make some supper for us."
They walked to the back of the house.
The cart clattered onto the cobblestones and stopped at the back door.
The children knocked but no one answered.
The cart driver said that Mrs. Viney had probably gone home.
The train had arrived very late.
"But she has the key!" Mother said.
"Oh, I'm sure she left it under the doorstep," the cart driver said.
"That's what people do around here."
He took the lantern off his cart and bent down.
"Here it is, sure enough!"
He unlocked the door.
The cart driver put down his lantern and lit a candle.
The kitchen was large, with a stone floor.
The table was in the middle.
The chairs, pots, pans, and crockery were in all corners of the room.
There was no fire, just cold ashes.
A rustling sound came from inside the walls.
"Oh, what's that?" cried the girls.
"It's only the rats," said the cart driver.
He left and shut the door, and a sudden wind blew out the candle.
"Oh dear," said Phyllis, "I wish we hadn't come!"
And she knocked a chair over.
"Only the rats!" said Peter in the dark.
"What fun!" said Mother, feeling for the matches on the table.
"I'm sure they are mice, not rats!"
She struck a match and everyone looked at each other.
"Well," Mother said, "you've often wanted something to happen and now it has.
This is quite an adventure, isn't it?
Let's go and eat the supper Mrs. Viney made."
The dining room was next to the kitchen.
The kitchen was white.
But the dining room was made of dark wood from floor to ceiling.
There was a table and chairs, but there was no supper.
"Let's look in the other rooms," said Mother, and they looked.
In each room there were furniture and boxes, but nothing to eat.
Even in the pantry there was only a rusty cake tin.
"What a horrible woman!" said Mother.
"She's taken the money but got us nothing to eat at all!"
"Then we can't have any supper," said Phyllis unhappily.
"Yes, we can," said Mother.
"We can unpack one of the boxes.
There's some food from the old house."
They were all very, very tired, but they cheered up at their unusual supper.
There were biscuits, sardines, raisins, and jam.
After supper they put sheets and blankets on the beds.
"Good night, darlings," said Mother.
"I'm sure there aren't any rats.
But I'll leave my door open, and if a mouse comes, you can scream.
I'll come and tell the mouse to go away!"
Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis were not convinced by her answer.
They left candles burning and spent the first night in their new home.
Very early the next morning, Bobbie pulled Phyllis' hair to wake her.
"Wake up!" Bobbie said.
"We're in the new house, remember?
We don't have any servants.
Let's get up and surprise Mother.
We'll clean up and make breakfast!
I've already awakened Peter."
The girls got dressed, lit the fire, and put the kettle on.
They set the table but could not find all the right dishes.
So they put salt in an ashtray and bread in a baking tin.
Then they went with Peter to look outside.
The house stood in a field on a hill, and the children could see a long way.
At the bottom of the hill was the railway line and a tunnel.
"This place is much prettier than our house in London," Phyllis said.
The station was too far away to see.
"Let's go and watch the trains passing," suggested Peter.
"We can see them from here," said Bobbie.
"Let's sit down for a bit."
So Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis sat down on a big comfortable stone in the grass.
When Mother came to look for them at eight o'clock, she found them asleep in the sun.
The children had made a fire earlier and put the kettle on.
But by the time Mother got up, the fire was out.
The water had boiled away, and the kettle was burnt.
"It doesn't matter.
I've got everything ready," said Mother.
"I found a little room that we missed last night in the darkness."
They went into the small room, which was next to the kitchen.
On the table Mrs. Viney had left roast beef, bread, butter, cheese, and apple pie.
"Pie for breakfast!" cried Peter happily.
Later Mother and the children unpacked and arranged their things in the rooms.
It was late in the afternoon when Mother said, "That's enough work for today.
I'm going to lie down for an hour, before supper."
The children looked at each other.
"What should we do?"
asked Bobbie, although she already knew the answer.
"Let's go to the railway!" cried Peter.
At the bottom of the hill there was a wooden fence.
The children climbed over it.
There was the railway, with its shiny tracks, telegraph wires and posts, and signals.
Just then the children heard a loud rumbling sound.
A train came out of the tunnel.
The pebbles on the track rattled and jumped as the train went by.
"Ooh!" said Bobbie slowly.
"It was like a great dragon going by and fanning us with its hot wings."
"Yes, I didn't think we'd be able to get so close to the trains!
That was amazing!" said Peter.
"I wonder if the train was going to London.
That's where Father is," said Phyllis.
"Let's find out!" said Peter, and so they ran to the station.
They walked along the tracks, counted the telegraph posts, and jumped up onto the station platform.
On one side of the station yard was a huge pile of coal for the steam trains.
There was a white line behind the coal, at the top of the pile.
Peter asked the station porter about the line.
"It's to show how much coal is there.
Then we know if anybody steals some!" the porter said, smiling.
Peter thought he was a nice, friendly person.
When the children left, they were excited at the thought of coming back soon.
For the next few weeks, the children happily explored outdoors.
Now that they were living in the country, they had stopped going to school.
Mother was mostly in her room, writing stories.
She sold stories for money because she said the family was poor now.
The children still had nice clothes and there was enough to eat, so they didn't mind.
They did not forget their father, but they had stopped talking about him.
They knew such talk made Mother unhappy.
In June it rained for three days.
It was very cold, and nobody went outside.
One day they went up to Mother's room.
"Can we light a fire?" Bobbie asked. "It's freezing!"
"I'm sorry, Bobbie, coal is too expensive," Mother replied.
"But Mother, we only need a little coal to make a fire!" Bobbie pleaded.
"We can't afford it!" said Mother.
"Please run along. I'm busy."
"Mother is always busy," Phyllis whispered to Peter.
Peter shrugged. He was thinking.
After tea Peter told his sisters, "I have an idea."
"What's your idea?" Bobbie asked.
"I won't tell you," was Peter's answer.
"Oh, very well," said Bobbie.
"Don't then," Phyllis said. "We don't care."
Peter looked angry and said, "There's a reason why I won't tell you.
My idea might be wrong."
"Don't do it if it's wrong," Bobbie replied.
"No," said Peter, "I'm going to do it.
Some people might think it's wrong, but I don't think it is.
If Mother asks where I am, tell her I'm playing a game called 'coal mining.'"
Two days later Peter said, "Come quickly, and bring the pram!"
Earlier they had seen an old pram in a shed behind the house.
The girls got it and followed Peter to the train station.
On the hill above the station, there was a small pile of coal in the grass.
"I just found the coal," said Peter.
"Help me carry it to the house."
Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis packed the pram full of coal and made three trips to the house.
They put the coal in the pile by the back door.
Afterward Peter went out alone.
He came back dirty and looking mysterious.
Peter went out every night, and the children told nobody.
A week later Mrs. Viney said that there was more coal than she thought.
The children were very happy—so happy they forgot Peter's actions might be wrong.
Then came the awful night when the stationmaster hid in the shadows.
He watched Peter climb onto the coal pile.
"Now I've caught you, thief!" shouted the stationmaster.
He grabbed Peter's jacket.
"Come with me to the station!"
"I'm not a thief," said Peter, but his voice shook.
"The police station?" said another voice.
The voice was Bobbie's.
Bobbie and Phyllis stepped out of the darkness.
"It was our fault too," Bobbie said.
The stationmaster looked at them.
"You're all from the white house on the hill.
Why are you stealing coal?" he asked.
"I didn't think it was stealing.
There's so much coal here," said Peter.
"Mother says we're too poor to have a fire."
The stationmaster thought for a minute and said, "I won't do anything this time.
But remember, this is the railway's coal.
Taking the coal is stealing."
The children nodded.
They knew he was right.
The children stayed away from the station, but they could not keep away from the railway.
They soon got to know the trains that passed by and gave names to them.
The 9:15 was the "Green Dragon," and the 10:07 was the "Winchester Worm."
One morning they sat on the hill and waited for the Green Dragon.
"The Green Dragon is going to London," said Phyllis.
"If it was a real dragon, we could stop it.
We could ask it to take our love to Father."
"Dragons don't carry people's love," said Peter.
"They're too fierce."
"Yes, they do, if you tame them first.
They fetch things like dogs," said Phyllis.
"And feed out of your hand.
I wonder why Father never writes to us."
"Mother says he's been too busy," said Bobbie.
"But he'll write soon, she says."
"Let's all wave to the Green Dragon as it goes by," Phyllis suggested.
"It will take our love to Father."
The children waved their handkerchiefs at the train . . . and a hand waved back!
It held a newspaper.
It was the hand of an old gentleman.
He was a nice-looking old man with white hair and a top hat.
Every day the children waved, and he waved back.
All this time Mother was very busy with her writing.
She sent off many envelopes with stories in them, and she received many envelopes too.
Sometimes she opened them and said, "Oh, dear," and the children were sorry.
But sometimes Mother would wave the envelope in the air and say,
"The magazine bought my story!" and she would buy buns for tea.
One day Peter was going to the village for buns when he saw the stationmaster.
"Good morning," said the stationmaster in a friendly way.
"G-g-good morning," said Peter nervously.
"I haven't seen you at the station for a while," said the stationmaster.
"After the trouble with the coal . . . ," began Peter.
"That's over now.
Come to the station whenever you like!" the stationmaster said, smiling.
"Oh, thank you," said Peter.
The next day the children waved to the Green Dragon.
Afterward Peter led his sisters to the station.
"But should we go?
After what happened with the coal?" said Phyllis doubtfully.
"I met the stationmaster yesterday and he said we could go any time we like," Peter replied.
At the station the children saw Perks, the porter.
Unlike some adults, Perks didn't mind answering endless questions beginning with "Why?"
He also told them many things about the railway.
They learned there was a man who wrote down the number of every train he saw.
Peter thought he could keep track of the trains' numbers too.
Perks gave him an envelope to write on.
Peter wrote down 379 and 663.
Later, at home, Peter asked his mother for a proper notebook.
She gave him one and said, "I'm so glad you like the railway.
But please don't walk on the tracks."
"Not even if we face the way the train is coming?" asked Phyllis.
"No," said Mother.
Bobbie said, "Mother, didn't you ever walk on the tracks when you were little?"
Mother was honest, so she had to say,
"Yes, I did . . . Okay, walk on the tracks, but not in tunnels or near corners."
The children smiled.
The next day Mother stayed in bed because her head ached so badly.
She had a fever and would not eat anything.
Dr. Forest came and said it was the flu.
"Nurse Bobbie," the doctor said, smiling at Bobbie.
"I'll send some medicine later.
Please give your mother this list—she needs beef soup, fresh fruit, and brandy."
When the doctor had gone, Bobbie showed Mother the piece of paper.
"Impossible!" Mother said with a laugh.
"We can't buy all these things!
We're poor, remember?"
"Yes, Mother," Bobbie answered and tried to smile.
The children talked later.
"Mother needs those things," said Bobbie.
"How can we get them for her?
Think, everybody, as hard as you can."
A plan was formed.
Phyllis and Peter found a white sheet, some black paint, and a paintbrush.
Bobbie stayed with Mother all night long.
The next morning the doctor came again.
"Everything going all right, little nurse?" Dr. Forest said in the hall.
"Did you get the brandy and fruit for your mother?"
"No, I couldn't. But I'll get them tomorrow," Bobbie said.
"Very well, then," the doctor replied.
When the 9:15 train came out of the tunnel that same morning, the old gentleman was ready to wave.
But instead of three children on the fence, there was just one: Peter.
But he was not waving.
Instead Peter was pointing at the large white sheet attached to the fence.
On the sheet were thick black letters that read:
Look Out at the Station.
Many passengers looked out their windows at the station, but they saw nothing peculiar.
But as the train was departing, the old gentleman saw Phyllis running toward him.
"I thought I was going to miss you!" she shouted.
She quickly thrust a letter into his hand through the window as the train moved away.
The old gentleman relaxed in his seat and opened the letter:
Dear Mr. (we do not know your name),
Mother is ill.
The doctor says we must give her good food.
But we don't have any money because Father is away.
Can you help us?
We can repay you.
From Roberta, Peter, and Phyllis
Below their names they had written down their requests.
That evening Perks came to their house with a big parcel.
Inside were all the things they had asked for.
There were also some things they had not asked for—wine, two chickens, and flowers.
There was a letter too.
Children,
Here is the food for your mother.
If she says you were wrong to ask for the things, tell her that I say you were right.
I was pleased to help.
The old man's name was underneath, but it was illegible.
"I think we were right," said Phyllis.
"Of course, we were right," said Bobbie.
"I hope Mother thinks we were right too," said Peter.
But he didn't sound very sure.
Two weeks later the old gentleman saw something different from the train window.
It was another white sheet with black letters.
It said: Mother Is Much Better. Thank You.
The children decided to tell Mother what they had done.
Mother was extremely angry and then suddenly she began to cry.
Crying is contagious, like measles, and soon everyone was crying.
Mother stopped first.
She dried her eyes and said, "I'm sorry I was angry, I know you tried to help.
It's true that we're poor, but you must not tell everyone.
And you must never ask strangers to give you things."
"We didn't mean to be naughty," cried Bobbie.
"We're sorry," said Phyllis and Peter, still crying too.
"I'll write a letter to the old gentleman and thank him for his kindness," Mother said, hugging them.
"You can give it to the stationmaster to give him.
And we won't talk about it anymore."
Afterward, when the children were alone, Bobbie said,
"Isn't Mother good?
Other grown-ups aren't sorry after they're angry."
"Yes," agreed Peter, "but it's awful when she's angry."
The day after they took the letter to the station was Bobbie's birthday.
In the afternoon she was politely told to stay outside until teatime.
"You mustn't see what we're doing.
It's a surprise," said Phyllis.
Bobbie went into the garden.
When she came back, Phyllis and Peter met her at the back door and led her to the front room.
They were unusually clean, and Phyllis had a red bow in her hair.
They stood with Mother near the table.
There were 12 lit candles on the table because Bobbie was turning 12.
The table held buns and jam and a big cake.
There were also flowers from the garden, and interesting little packages.
"Happy Birthday, Bobbie!" they shouted happily.
"Open your presents!"
They were very nice presents.
There was a dainty handkerchief from Phyllis.
There was also a silver brooch of Mother's, shaped like a rose.
Bobbie had admired it for a long time.
Mrs. Viney gave Bobbie a vase.
"This is my present,"
said Peter, placing his toy steam engine on the table.
It was full of sweets.
Bobbie was surprised.
Peter was giving her his treasured engine?
"Not the engine," he said quickly. "Only the sweets."
But Peter had seen the look on Bobbie's face.
"I mean, not all the engine.
You . . . you can have half, if you like," he said bravely.
"Thanks, Peter," said Bobbie. "It's a wonderful present."
And Bobbie thought, "It was very kind of Peter to give me half his engine.
Well, I'll have the broken half, and I'll get it fixed."
"And now look at the cake," said Mother.
Bobbie looked more closely at the cake.
On top was something that looked like a pattern, made with flowers.
"What is it?" asked Bobbie.
"It's a map—a map of the railway!" said Peter.
After tea Mother played games with them.
It was a lovely birthday.
Later that night Bobbie crept downstairs to get her presents.
Bobbie saw Mother sitting at the table, with a pen and some writing paper.
"She's writing to Father," thought Bobbie.
But she saw Mother wasn't writing.
Mother's head rested on her arms on the table.
"It's my birthday, and she doesn't want me to know she's unhappy," thought Bobbie.
She went quietly back to her room.
But it was a sad end to her birthday.
The next morning Bobbie thought about how to get the train engine repaired in secret.
The chance came that afternoon.
Mother was going to the nearest town to do some shopping.
Peter, Bobbie, and Phyllis were accompanying her.
Bobbie wanted an excuse to stay home, but she couldn't think of one.
As they were leaving, her dress caught on a nail by the door.
Mother said there was no time to change her dress.
So Bobbie could not go with them.
Hooray! Bobbie changed into an ordinary dress and went down to the railway.
She walked along the tracks and past the platform.
When she reached the place where the engines stopped, she hid behind a bush.
Bobbie had the toy engine wrapped up in brown paper.
She waited patiently with it.
When the next train came in and stopped, she went and stood next to the engine.
She had never been so close to an engine before.
The engine driver and the stoker did not see her.
They were talking to Perks, the porter, who was on the other side of the tracks.
"Excuse me," began Bobbie.
But the men could not hear her because of the noise.
Bobbie climbed onto the engine's step so they could hear her.
At that moment the train began to move!
Bobbie fell inside, onto a pile of coal.
"Help! Help!" she cried.
But the men still didn't see her or hear her.
"I shouldn't be here," she thought as the train went faster.
"I'll be in big trouble!"
Bobbie put out her hand and touched the nearest arm, and the driver turned around quickly.
"What are you doing here?" he shouted.
Bobbie began to cry.
The men took several minutes to calm Bobbie down and stop her crying.
Then the stoker said, "Now, tell us why you're here.
It's not every day a little girl tumbles into our steam engine!"
Bobbie showed them Peter's toy engine.
"I . . . I wanted to ask you if you could fix this," she explained.
"Everybody on the railway is so nice.
I didn't think you'd mind."
The men examined the little engine. Bobbie waited.
"What do you think, Jim?" said the driver at last.
"Can we help the little lady?"
The stoker grinned. "I think we can."
"Oh, thank you!" cried Bobbie.
"But now we must get you home," said the driver.
Bobbie stayed on the train until the next station.
The men put her on another train and sent her home.
"Where have you been?" asked Phyllis and Peter.
"To the station, of course," said Bobbie.
But she would not say another word.
A few weeks later, Bobbie collected the toy engine.
Peter was very excited when he saw it.
It was as good as new.
Then Bobbie told them about her great engine adventure.
One day the children were walking by the fence along the top of the hill, beside the railway line.
The ground was very rocky, but some grass and small trees grew.
The children were looking for wild cherries.
Suddenly they heard a noise.
The noise was soft but very clear, and slowly it began to get louder.
"Look at the tree over there!" shouted Peter.
The girls looked and saw a tree moving slowly down the hill.
The tree was moving toward the railway line!
"It's magic!" said Phyllis. "I knew the railway was magic!
Look, some other trees are moving too!"
It really did seem like magic—all the trees seemed to be walking down the hillside!
A loud rumbling sound filled the air.
"Oh, I don't like it!
Let's go home!" said Phyllis.
But they all watched as the trees slipped slowly down the hillside.
Then some stones and loose earth fell down and rattled on the railway tracks far below.
A big rock began to move too.
"It's all coming down,"
Peter tried to say, but he was too scared to speak.
More rocks, grass, trees, and bushes slipped off the hill and crashed onto the tracks below.
A cloud of dust rose up.
"It's blocked the tracks!" cried Phyllis.
"Yes," said Peter, thinking.
"And the 11:29 hasn't gone past yet.
We must let them know at the station, or there will be a terrible accident," Bobbie said.
"There isn't time!" said Phyllis.
"It's after eleven now," Peter said.
They thought for a moment.
"We need something red to get people's attention," said Peter.
"Then we could go down and wave to the train."
They started to walk down the hill.
Bobbie was pale, and Phyllis was red-faced and worried.
"Oh, how hot I am!" she said.
"I thought it was going to be cold.
I wish we hadn't put on our . . ."
She stopped suddenly and looked excited.
"Our petticoats!" Phyllis cried.
"They're red! Let's take them off!"
The girls took off their petticoats, and the three children ran to the sharp bend in the railway line.
The train would be coming soon.
"Now," said Peter, taking hold of the largest flannel petticoat.
"You're not . . . you're not going to tear them?" asked Phyllis.
"Phyllis, if we can't stop the train, there'll be a real accident, with people killed!" Bobbie said.
Peter divided each petticoat into three pieces.
Then he looked at his watch again.
"We've got seven minutes.
We'll need some sticks as well."
They found some sticks and tied the flannel onto them.
Now they had six red flags.
The children made two little piles of rocks on the tracks, and stuck a red flag in each.
Then Phyllis and Bobbie each took a flag.
"I will have two flags because I'm the one who tore them," said Peter.
"They're our petticoats though," Phyllis began to argue.
But Bobbie interrupted.
"Who cares? We have to save the train!"
Perhaps Peter's watch was slow, or perhaps the train was late.
They seemed to wait for a long time.
It seemed as if the children had been standing next to the tracks for hours, holding their little flannel flags.
They had to warn the train to stop before it came around the bend and crashed into the rocks and trees!
"Maybe Peter's watch is wrong, and the train has already gone by," said Phyllis impatiently.
But at last came a distant hum and a puff of white steam.
"Wave your flags!" Peter shouted.
"And Bobbie, don't stand on the tracks!"
The train came rattling along, very, very fast.
"They don't see us!
It's no good!" cried Bobbie.
The two flags sitting on the tracks swayed as the train approached.
Then one tipped forward and fell onto the tracks.
Bobbie jumped forward, and caught the flag, and waved it.
The train came as fast as ever.
It was very close now.
"Keep off the tracks, Bobbie!" Peter warned her.
"It's no good," said Bobbie again.
"Stand back, Bobbie!" shouted Phyllis.
But Bobbie cried, "Not yet, not yet!" and stood right on the tracks.
She waved her two flags.
The front of the engine looked black and very big.
"Oh, stop, stop, stop!" cried Bobbie.
But no one heard her.
Peter and Phyllis didn't hear Bobbie because of the noise of the train.
But afterward Bobbie wondered if the engine had heard her because it slowed down quickly and stopped twenty meters in front of Bobbie.
Bobbie saw the great black engine stop, but she could not stop waving the flags.
The engine driver and the fireman jumped off the train.
Peter and Phyllis ran to meet them.
Bobbie couldn't move because her legs were shaking too much.
When the others came back to get Bobbie, she was lying on the ground, still gripping the little red flannel flags.
She had fainted. The engine driver picked her up.
He carried her into a first-class car, where he laid her down on some cushions.
"I think that's what people look like when they're dead," Phyllis whispered.
"Don't say that!" said Peter sharply.
The train started up again and went back to the station.
Soon Bobbie sighed and opened her eyes.
Then she rolled over and began to cry.
This cheered up Peter and Phyllis because they had seen her cry before.
But they had never seen her faint.
When the train reached the station, a small crowd of people greeted Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis as heroes.
The children were praised for their bravery and quick thinking.
"You're brave and clever children," the driver told them.
Phyllis enjoyed the attention.
She had never been a heroine before.
Peter's ears got very red, but he was happy.
Only Bobbie wished they could all leave at that moment.
"You'll hear from the train company about this, I expect," the stationmaster said.
Bobbie wished she would never hear of it again.
She pulled at Peter's jacket.
"Come on! I want to go home!" Bobbie said.
She kept thinking about the pile of rocks on the track.
What would have happened had the train crashed into it?
And so they went home.
As the children left the station, the stationmaster, guards, and drivers cheered.

episodes.title: A Special Day at the Station

subtitle.text: For many nights after the children saved the train, Bobbie woke up screaming with nightmares.
One morning a letter arrived.
It was addressed to Peter, Bobbie, and Phyllis.
Curious, they opened the letter quickly. It said:
Dear Sir and Ladies,
Thank you for saving the train and stopping a very bad accident.
Please come to the station at three o'clock, on the 30th of the month.
Yours faithfully, J. Inglewood
Secretary of the Great Northern and Southern Railway Company
It was to be a special day indeed.
The children went to the station at three o'clock, dressed in their best clothes.
The stationmaster came to meet them.
"Come into the waiting room," he said.
The waiting room looked very different today.
There was a carpet on the floor and roses on the windowsills.
Green branches hung from the wall.
Perks, the porter, was there, as well as several men with tall hats.
There were ladies in expensive dresses too.
Best of all, the old gentleman from the train was there.
He came across the room to shake the children's hands.
Then an important-looking man stood up.
He spoke about how bravely the children had acted.
Next the old gentleman got up and said nice things about the children too.
Then he called the children one by one, and gave each of them a beautiful gold watch and chain.
Inside the watches there was a message.
You were very brave.Thank
you for stopping a train accident. From
the Directors of the Railway Company .
The stationmaster whispered to Bobbie, "Now you must make a speech and thank everyone," and he gently pushed Bobbie forward.
"Oh dear," said Bobbie.
"Ladies and gentlemen," she began, "thank you for these lovely watches.
We really don't deserve them, because what we did wasn't anything really.
Well, it was exciting and frightening . . . Oh, thank you all very much!"
The people clapped, and then everybody shook hands with the three children.
It was a wonderful day.
Afterward the old gentleman walked with them to their little white house.
"I want to meet the mother of these brave and clever children," he said.
Mother was surprised to see their visitor.
She thanked the old man again for the things he had sent when she was ill.
While they had tea and buns, the children told Mother about the people at the station.
Mother and the old gentleman chatted in French and English.
When it was time for the old gentleman to leave, Mother said,
"Lovely to meet you.
I want to thank you for everything."
Then the children waved good-bye to the old gentleman.
It was just as they did every morning when his train passed by.
One day Mother rode the train to the next town to go shopping.
The children went to the station to meet her when she returned.
Because they loved the station so much, they arrived an hour early.
They sat in the waiting room.
When a train arrived, Peter, Phyllis, and Bobbie rushed out to see it.
They expected to see just one or two people, but instead the platform was crowded.
They could not see anything but people's backs and elbows.
Everybody was talking at once.
It was clear that something had happened.
"If you ask me," one man said, "he looks odd.
We should call the police."
"No, call the hospital!" a lady said.
Then the stationmaster said loudly, "Everybody, move along!"
But the crowd did not move.
Suddenly the children heard an unusual voice.
A man was speaking a foreign language—a language the children had never heard before.
"What's he saying?" someone asked.
"Sounds like French to me," said the stationmaster.
"It isn't French," said Peter.
"I know what French sounds like."
The crowd parted to see who had spoken, and now Peter could see the man.
He wore strange clothes, and had long hair and wild eyes.
"Well, try speaking to the man if you know so much," said one lady to Peter.
Just then the man ran forward, grabbed Peter's hands, and began speaking to him in French.
"What's he saying?" the stationmaster asked.
"I don't know," answered Peter.
The stationmaster took the man into the waiting room.
"Mother can speak French," Bobbie said to the stationmaster.
"She'll arrive on the next train."
As they waited with the man, Peter got an idea.
He pulled an envelope out of his pocket.
It was full of foreign stamps.
Peter showed the man an Italian stamp, pointing from the stamp to him.
But the man shook his head.
Next the children showed him a Norwegian stamp and a Spanish stamp.
Again the man shook his head.
At last he took the envelope and searched among the stamps himself.
"He's Russian!" Phyllis exclaimed as the man held up a Russian stamp.
By now Mother's train had arrived, and the stationmaster brought her into the waiting room.
The Russian stood up and bowed.
Mother spoke in French and he replied, a little at first, but then in longer sentences.
The children watched Mother's face.
They could see that he was telling her things that made her angry and sad.
"Well, it's all right," Mother finally reported.
"He lost his ticket.
And I'm afraid he's very sick.
If you don't mind, I'll take him home with me now."
"You should be careful, ma'am!" said the stationmaster.
"Oh no," said Mother brightly.
"He's a great man in Russia.
He writes books, beautiful books."
They all went home, and the Russian man went to sleep in Mother's room.
It was the only room with a fireplace.
Later Bobbie showed the doctor into the room.
Inside she spotted Mother's big black suitcase.
It was usually locked, but now it was open.
There were men's clothes in it—her father's clothes.
Why hadn't Father taken his clothes?
Bobbie's heart was beating horribly.
Bobbie ran to the kitchen.
"Mother . . . Daddy isn't . . . isn't dead, is he?"
"My darling, no! What makes you think of something so horrible?"
"I . . . I don't know."
Bobbie didn't mention the clothes she'd seen in her mother's suitcase.
Mother gave her a quick hug.
"Daddy was quite well when I heard from him last," she said.
"And he will come back to us one day.
Don't think such horrible things!"
Later Mother came into the girls' room.
She was going to sleep there, in Phyllis' bed.
Peter was also there.
"Now, Mother," said Peter, "tell us about the Russian gentleman.
We have been patient.
Make a nice long story of it."
"I can't make a long story of it tonight," said Mother.
"I'm very tired."
Bobbie could tell from Mother's voice that Mother had been crying.
But the others didn't know.
"Well, make it as long as you can," said Phyllis, and Bobbie snuggled up to Mother.
"Well," began Mother.
"This man, Mr. Schepansky, wrote a book about how to help poor people.
In Russia, criticizing wealthy people is against the rules of the czar.
So Mr. Schepansky was sent to prison for three years in Siberia."
"But Mother, that can't be true," cried Peter.
"It is true, my dears," Mother said.
"He was sent to prison because of his ideas.
He had not done any crime.
The prisoners work in the mines in the cold winters.
If someone is sick, they are left to die."
"How did he get away?" asked Phyllis.
"He escaped," Mother said.
"His wife and children left Russia and came to England.
But he doesn't know where they are.
When he finds his family, maybe they can live together here."
Then Mother looked sad and said, "Let's say a prayer for all prisoners."
They did that and went to bed.
But Bobbie stayed up for a while.
She had decided to write a letter to the old gentleman.
She asked him to meet her the next morning:
My dearest Old Gentleman,
I really want to ask you something.
I do not want you to give me anything.
Mother says that is wrong.
I only want to talk with you about a prisoner.
Please get off the train tomorrow so we can talk.
Your little friend, Bobbie
The next morning Bobbie was waiting when the old gentleman got off the train.
"Well," said the old gentleman, tapping Bobbie's shoulder, "what is it?"
"Oh! You came!" replied Bobbie, turning round.
"Well . . ." And she told him the story of the Russian.
"Oh!" the old gentleman exclaimed.
"I've read his book.
It's translated into every European language.
It's a noble book.
I'll do my best to help him."
"I was sure you could help!" said Bobbie excitedly. "Thank you."
Ten days later the three children sat on the hill watching the 5:15 steam past.
When they saw the old gentleman get off the train, they ran to meet him.
"Good news!" he said.
"I've found the Russian writer's family!
You run and tell him."
Bobbie ran home ahead and told the news to Mother and the Russian.
The Russian man cried with happiness.
That day he left for London and was reunited with his wife and children.
There was a canal near the children's house.
Small boats called barges went up and down the canal.
The boats often carried coal.
Some boats had motors and some were pulled by horses or mules.
The children loved the canal almost as much as the railway.
They loved the railway best for two reasons.
They had found the railway first, and the people who worked on the canal barges were unfriendly.
Once the children had gone fishing in the canal.
But a boy on a barge had thrown a piece of coal at Phyllis.
He'd done it just for fun.
What a nasty boy!
Phyllis said it didn't hurt, but they stopped fishing and went home.
One fine day the three children were walking along the road near the canal.
Peter said, "Let's go fishing again!"
Phyllis remembered the mean boy.
But Peter said, "I'll fight any boys who throw coal at your head, Phyllis!"
So they went down to the path next to the canal and started fishing.
The children fished for half an hour.
"Hey!" said a loud voice. "Move!"
An old white horse walked slowly toward them.
It was pulling a barge.
Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis jumped off the path and climbed up the hill.
They waited for the barge and the horse to pass so they could keep fishing.
"The barge is staying here! What rotten luck!" said Peter.
The man on the barge looked at them and said angrily, "What are you staring at?"
"We weren't staring," said Bobbie.
"Well, go away!" said the man.
"We can stay here.
We're not bothering anyone!" said Phyllis.
"You're bothering me!" said the man.
He got off his barge and started to climb the hill.
The children were a little scared.
The bargeman grabbed Peter's leg and said, "You can't fish in the canal.
And don't be so cheeky!"
Bobbie came down the hill a little and talked to the bargeman.
"Please don't be angry with Peter.
We won't fish anymore."
"All right then.
Now go home," he replied.
The man went down to his barge.
"Give me a coat, Maria!" he shouted.
A red-haired woman with a baby threw a coat at him.
"I'll be at the pub, the Rose and Crown.
Meet me there when the baby's asleep," he said.
When the bargeman had gone, the children climbed down the hill.
"I think the canal belongs to everyone," Peter said.
The woman got off the boat and saw them.
"Don't worry about Bill," she said.
"He gets angry quickly.
He'll be back in two hours.
You can catch fish now," she said.
"Thank you," said Bobbie.
"You're kind. Where's your baby?"
"Asleep in the cabin," she replied.
"He'll be fine.
He's safe in there, and the dog's with him."
The woman left, and Peter fished for a while, but he didn't catch anything.
It was nearly dark, and the girls were tired.
Suddenly Phyllis cried, "What's that?"
She pointed to the barge.
Smoke poured from the doors.
"The bargeman's boat is on fire, that's all.
I'm glad!" said Peter.
"Peter, how can you say that?" cried Phyllis.
"Think of the poor dog!"
"And the baby!" Bobbie suddenly screamed.
All three children ran to the barge as fast as they could.
Smoke was rising from the barge.
Bobbie climbed onto the barge and then Peter did too.
But he slipped and fell into the canal.
The water was up to Peter's neck!
He could not feel the bottom of the canal with his feet.
While Peter gripped the edge of the barge, Phyllis reached over and pulled him by the hair.
It hurt, but she managed to pull him out of the water.
Peter jumped onto the barge.
And then Bobbie helped Phyllis on too.
Bobbie went toward the cabin door, but Peter shouted, "Not you!
I should go because I'm wet."
He pushed her away.
Normally she would have cried because Peter was so rough.
But today she only said, "No, Peter, I'll go!"
Peter rushed past her down the stairs, into a thick cloud of smoke.
He stopped and tied his wet handkerchief over his mouth.
Then he called out to Bobbie, "It's all right, there's hardly any fire!"
He lied because he didn't want Bobbie coming down.
Inside, the cabin glowed red.
Peter lifted the handkerchief from his mouth and called, "Baby, where are you?"
He choked from the smoke.
"Let me look!" cried Bobbie from behind him.
Peter pushed her back.
At that moment the baby cried out.
Peter felt his way through the dark smoke and found something small and alive.
He picked it up and bumped into Bobbie.
The dog barked at him.
"I've got the baby," Peter said and ran upstairs.
Bobbie listened to the sound of the barking and then felt around for the dog's head.
The dog put his teeth on her hand, but very gently.
Bobbie said, "Come on," and she carried the dog up.
Peter and Bobbie climbed off the barge with the baby and dog.
"Give me the baby, Peter," Bobbie said.
"You're so wet, you'll give it a cold.
Now run to the pub quickly!"
"I can't run in these wet clothes!" said Peter. "They're heavy."
"Then I'll go! Phyllis, take the baby," Bobbie said and ran toward the Rose and Crown pub.
Inside the pub a group of barge workers sat drinking beer.
Bobbie burst in and cried out, "Bill! I want Bill the bargeman!"
There was silence.
People held their glasses in midair.
Bobbie saw Maria, Bill's wife.
"Your barge is on fire," she cried. "Go quickly."
The woman jumped to her feet and cried out, "Little Harry!
Oh my dear little Harry!"
"Your baby is safe," said Bobbie. "The dog's safe too."
Bill, the bargeman, leaped to his feet and ran with his wife to the canal.
Bill jumped onto the barge with buckets of water.
Peter helped him, and they put out the fire.
Mother was very worried until the children finally arrived at the house.
It was late at night and they were soaking wet.
She listened to their story and let them accept Bill's thank-you present.
It was a ride on the barge the next day.
Phyllis, Bobbie, and Peter went to the canal the next morning.
In a basket they had bread and cheese and ham for lunch.
They spent all day on Bill's barge, going up and down the canal, in the warm sunshine.
Mr. Bill was very nice to them.
He told the children they could fish anytime, and he would help them.
When the children told Mother, she said,
"So you've made more friends.
First at the railway and now at the canal!"
The children were drinking tea with Mr. Perks in the porter's room at the station.
They had brought their own cups and some biscuits.
Perks made tea in a beer can as usual, and everyone was happy and talkative.
"When is your birthday, Mr. Perks?" Bobbie asked him.
"My birthday?" asked Perks.
"I gave up birthdays before you were born!"
"But you must have been born at some time," said Phyllis thoughtfully.
"Even if it was twenty years ago—or sixty or seventy!"
"Not that long ago, missy!" Perks grinned as he answered.
"Actually, I'll be 32 on the fifteenth of this month."
Later the children talked.
Perks was the best friend they had made.
So they decided to do something special for his birthday.
The next day at breakfast Mother smiled as she gave the children porridge and milk.
"I've sold another story," she said, "so there'll be buns for tea."
Phyllis, Bobbie, and Peter looked at each other.
They were thinking the same thing.
"Mother, can we have buns on the fifteenth instead?" Bobbie asked.
"It's Perks' birthday, and we thought we'd have a small party."
"Yes, you can," Mother replied."We'll
put his name on the buns with icing!" The
children looked excited. Later
Bobbie said, "I think we need flowers as well." "Yes,
we need more ideas! Let's
all be quiet and think," said Phyllis. "Hooray!"
Peter cried suddenly. "I've
got it!" He jumped up. "What?"
said his sisters eagerly. "Well,
Perks is so nice to everybody. There
must be lots of people in the village who'd like to give presents to Perks. Let's
go round and ask everyone." "Mother
said we shouldn't ask people for things," said Bobbie doubtfully. "For
ourselves, silly, not for other people," said Peter. So
they went. The old lady at the post office didn't want to give Perks a present.
"It's my birthday tomorrow and nobody cares about it," she said.
"Why should I care about Perks' birthday?"
The children left and went elsewhere.
Some people were kind and some were not.
At the end of the day, Peter wrote a list of things they'd received.
He wrote it in the book where he kept the numbers of train engines.
Presents Given:
a pipe from the sweet shop
some tea from the village store
Presents Promised:
some meat from the butcher
six eggs from the farmer
a spade from the blacksmith
Early the next morning, Bobbie woke Phyllis.
They had a plan but had not told Peter.
He would think it was silly.
They cut a bunch of roses and wrote a card:
"For Mrs. Ransome, Happy Birthday."
Bobbie and Phyllis took the roses and card to the post office.
They put them on the counter before the old lady came in.
When they got home, Peter was telling Mother about their plan to give Perks gifts for his birthday.
"It depends on how you give him the presents," Mother said.
"I hope he won't be offended and think it's charity.
Poor people are very proud, you know."
"It isn't because he's poor," said Phyllis.
"It's because we like him very much."
The morning of the fifteenth, the children watched Mother decorate the buns with pink icing.
Then they went to the village to collect the spade and eggs and other things people had promised.
They passed the old lady at the post office.
"Thank you for the roses," she said.
"Here, take these for Perks' birthday present."
She brought out a basket full of red gooseberries.
"And wait one more moment.
I have something else for Perks!"
The children smiled.
Perks was going to have the best birthday ever!
The old lady at the post office said to Bobbie, Phyllis, and Peter, "You're good little children.
Here's a pram I'm not using.
I bought it for my daughter's first baby, but he died at six months old.
I'd like Mrs. Perks to have the pram for her baby," she said.
Phyllis hugged the old lady and said, "Oh, Perks will be pleased!"
They packed all the gifts into the pram and took it to Perks' house.
The garden was very tidy.
A jug of daisies sat on the windowsill.
Bobbie knocked on the door.
Mrs. Perks came out.
"We've got some presents for Mr. Perks' birthday," said Peter.
As they unpacked the presents, Mrs. Perks gasped.
She surprised everyone by suddenly bursting into tears.
"Oh don't!" said the children.
Peter said impatiently, "What's the matter?"
Mrs. Perks only sobbed.
The Perks children stood at the door, looking uncomfortable.
There was an awkward silence.
Phyllis and Bobbie patted Mrs. Perks on the back.
She stopped crying and said, "Perks has never had a birthday like this, not even when he was little.
You children are very kind."
Mrs. Perks put the buns and berries on plates.
"Let's hide in the laundry, then come in and surprise Perks," whispered Bobbie.
They quickly ran into the laundry, but there wasn't time to close the door.
They had to push the young Perks children in front of them and all squeeze in together.
"Hello!" Perks called out.
"Isn't this pretty? It's your birthday tea," said Mrs. Perks.
There was the sound of a kiss.
"But what's that pram doing here?" said Perks.
"What are all these things?
Where did you get . . .?"
Mrs. Perks mumbled something.
"I don't care," Perks said angrily.
"We've been fine all these years.
I'm not going to accept charity now!"
"Shh!" said Mrs. Perks.
"The children can hear everything you say!"
"Good! I've got more to say to them!" he shouted.
"Come out! Tell me why you did this!
Did I say I needed anything?
Why am I receiving this charity?"
Perks sat down heavily in a chair and frowned.
"Oh," said Phyllis, "I thought you'd be pleased.
I'll never try to be kind again, I promise."
She burst into tears.
"We didn't mean to make you angry," Peter said.
"It's not what you mean, it's what you do," said Perks.
"But the presents are not all from us.
They're from people in the village," Bobbie said.
"And who asked for them?" said Perks.
"We did," said Phyllis.
"So you've told all the neighbors that we're poor and need charity?" asked Perks.
"Well, you can just take the pram and the gifts and go home."
He turned his chair around so that his back faced the children.
Then suddenly Bobbie spoke.
"The people in the village wanted to give you birthday presents."
Perks slowly turned his chair around to face the children.
He seemed a little less angry.
Bobbie kept talking in a quiet voice.
"The doctor said, 'I'm pleased to give something to Perks.
He always pays his bills.'"
Now Bobbie continued in a louder voice, "And the grocer said, 'Perks works hard.'
And the lady at the post office said that you always—"
"Stop," said Perks suddenly. "I take back every word.
I didn't understand.
I am pleased . . . not just with the presents, but with the kind thoughts of our neighbors.
They're the best presents of all, aren't they, Nell?"
His wife nodded.
Perks looked at the children.
"You'll stay for tea?"
"Yes, please!" they said.
When the children first moved into the white house, they talked about Father a lot.
They were always asking questions about him.
But as time passed, the questions seemed to make Mother unhappy.
So they stopped asking them.
One day, when Mother was working very hard, Bobbie carried some tea up to Mother's "workshop."
The room had hardly any furniture, just a table, a chair, and a rug.
But the children always put flowers on the windowsills.
Mother said, "You have all been so good, especially you, Bobbie.
Picking me flowers, cleaning my shoes, making my bed . . ."
Bobbie had sometimes wondered whether Mother noticed their efforts.
"That's nothing," Bobbie said, but she was very happy.
Mother had agreed to give the children each a piece of garden.
The children could plant whatever they liked.
Phyllis had planted flowers in hers.
When they grew, they looked like weeds, but Phyllis believed they would be flowers one day.
Peter sowed vegetable seeds in his garden—carrots and onions and turnips.
But the vegetables never grew.
That was because Peter used the dirt to make forts and canals for his toy soldiers.
Bobbie had planted rosebushes in her garden, but all the new leaves were brown.
She hoped they were not dead.
One day Perks came to see the garden.
He told her that the rosebushes should go in a bonfire.
"Dig them up and burn them, Miss Bobbie!" Perks said.
"I'll give you some flowers from my garden.
You can plant them instead."
So she started digging up her rosebushes and carried them to the end of the garden.
Bobbie came back and saw Peter using the rake.
"I was using the rake," she said.
"Well, I'm using it now," said Peter.
"But I had it first," said Bobbie.
"Then it's my turn now," said Peter, and the fight began.
"You're always annoyed about something," Peter said.
"I had the rake first," Bobbie said, holding its handle.
"Didn't I tell you this morning that I would be using it?
Didn't I say that, Phyllis?" Phyllis didn't answer.
"Phyllis, answer!" Peter said, but Phyllis didn't.
"I wish I'd had a brother instead of two sisters," Peter said.
Bobbie was angry.
Then she remembered she should try to be good.
She let go of the rake's handle suddenly.
Peter had been pulling at the rake, and now he fell backward.
Peter lay still for a minute—long enough to frighten Bobbie a little.
Then he sat up and screamed, and then lay down and cried steadily.
Mother ran outside and knelt beside Peter. "What happened?"
"Bobbie and Peter were both pulling the rake," replied Phyllis.
"She let go and he fell over."
"Peter, stop squealing," said Mother. "Are you hurt?"
"I think my foot's broken, that's all," said Peter.
Then Peter went quite white.
"He is hurt. He's fainted," Mother said.
She undid Peter's boots.
As she took his right boot off, something dripped from his foot to the ground.
It was red blood.
The bottom of the rake had gone into Peter's foot, and it was bleeding.
Mother carried him into the house, and Phyllis ran for the doctor.
Mother carried Peter inside.
His foot was bleeding, and his face was pale.
Dr. Forest bandaged his foot.
Bobbie whispered to the doctor.
"He won't be lame, or have to use crutches forever, will he?"
The doctor told her not to worry.
Over the next week, Peter rested and Phyllis played in the garden.
Meanwhile Bobbie thought about Father.
Why was he still away?
Was there something that Mother wasn't telling them?
The answer to Bobbie's questions came the next day.
She went to the station to get magazines for Peter.
They were old magazines that people had left on trains or in the waiting room.
Perks said the children could have them.
"I'll put some newspaper and string around the magazines to keep them together," Perks said.
He took an old newspaper from the pile and wrapped up the magazines.
On the way home, Bobbie stopped at the train crossing as a train went past.
Bobbie rested the parcel on the crossing gate.
She looked down at the newspaper on top and started to read a headline and . . .
It was like a horrible dream.
Bobbie ran home, went to her room, and locked the door.
Inside her room Bobbie took out the newspaper again.
The front page said:
Five Years in Prison for Spy!
And the name of the "spy" was her father.
"So now I know," she whispered to herself.
Then Bobbie had to eat dinner and pretend that nothing was wrong.
She tried, but she wasn't very successful.
Her eyes were red from crying.
"Is anything wrong?" Mother asked her.
"I'm all right," Bobbie said.
After dinner Mother went to Bobbie's room.
"What's the matter?" she wanted to know.
Bobbie showed her mother the newspaper.
"Oh, Bobbie!" cried Mother.
"You don't believe it, do you?
You don't think Daddy is a spy!"
"No!" Bobbie said.
"He's good and honest and he has done nothing wrong," said Mother.
"We must remember that."
"What happened?" asked Bobbie.
"Do you remember those two men who came to see Father?" said Mother.
"Well, they said he was a spy, and that he'd sold government secrets to another country.
There were some letters in Daddy's desk at his office.
When the police saw them, they were sure Daddy was a spy."
"But why were the letters in his desk?" asked Bobbie.
"Somebody put them there," replied Mother, "and that person is the real spy."
"Who?" asked Bobbie.
"We don't know."
"Can't you explain that Daddy is not a spy to the police?" said Bobbie.
"We tried, but they won't listen," said Mother sadly.
"I've tried everything.
All we can do is wait.
Now we can't talk about this anymore, and we can't tell Peter or Phyllis.
Please be brave, Bobbie."
Bobbie had to try to help Father somehow.
She wrote a letter to the old gentleman.
He had helped them before—maybe he could help them again.
Dear Friend,
Please read the newspaper.
The story is about our father, but it is not true.
Mother says someone put the letters in Father's desk, but nobody listens to her.
You are good and clever.
Can you find the real spy?
Peter and Phyllis don't know Father is in prison.
Please help me.
With love from your friend, Bobbie
Bobbie tore the first page from the newspaper and put it in the envelope with her letter.
She asked the stationmaster to please give it to the old gentleman the next morning.
Now all she could do was wait.
Would the old gentleman help her family again?
"The boys from the next town are playing Paper Chase today," said Bobbie one morning.
"Perks thinks they'll run along the railway line.
We can go and watch."
Mother gave the children some lunch, and they left.
There were men working on the tracks, using different tools like spades and shovels.
The children watched them for awhile. Then
a voice said, "Let me pass, please." It
was the first boy from the school. "He's
'it.'" Bobbie explained the game to her brother and sister. "All
the other boys have to chase after him." Under
the boy's arm was a bag full of little pieces of paper. The
boy dropped a piece of paper behind him for the other boys to follow. The
children watched as he ran into the long dark tunnel, dropping more paper behind him.
The workmen watched him too.
"He shouldn't go in there," said one.
"It's only a game," said another.
Then the other boys came, running and following the little white pieces of paper.
Bobbie and Phyllis and Peter counted the boys as they ran past.
There were thirty of them.
The boys ran into the tunnel and disappeared into the deep darkness.
The last boy wore a red shirt.
"It's not easy running in the dark," said one of the workmen.
"How long will it take?" Peter asked, eyeing the long tunnel.
It went through a hill.
"An hour or more," the man said.
"Let's go across the top of the hill," said Peter.
"We can watch the boys come out the other end."
The children climbed up the steep hill, over rocks and tree trunks.
"It's like climbing the Alps!" said Bobbie, out of breath.
At last they reached the top.
Peter lay down on the grass, and the girls lay down too.
After awhile Bobbie sat up. "Look!"
she cried. "What?"
said Phyllis. "The
view," said Bobbie. "Let's
go now," said Peter. "But
this view is fantastic!" insisted Bobbie. They
could see the fields, the village, the station and even their white house. "We'll
miss the paper chase!" said Phyllis impatiently. "Come
on. Let's go." They
climbed down until they were level with the top of the tunnel. They waited. "The
boys have all gone past already, of course," said Phyllis, annoyed. "I
don't think so," said Bobbie. "But
even if they have, there's a wonderful view here too! We
can see the trains come out of the tunnel. We've
never seen the trains from on top before."
"Look, here he comes!" Peter shouted at last.
The first boy with the paper came slowly out of the tunnel.
Soon after came the other boys.
Some looked very tired.
"What will we do now?" asked Bobbie.
"That's not the last one," Peter said.
"Where's the boy in the red shirt?"
They waited a long time, but the boy did not appear.
The children began to worry, and they climbed down to the train tracks.
"Perhaps he had an accident," said Phyllis.
"Let's go and look," said Bobbie.
They slowly walked a few steps into the dark tunnel.
But they couldn't see a boy in a red shirt.
It was very dark and water dripped down the wall.
"I don't like it in here!" said Phyllis, looking frightened.
Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis were walking slowly inside the tunnel.
They were looking for the boy in the red shirt.
Unlike the other boys, he had not come out of the tunnel.
"If a train comes, stand flat against the wall," said Bobbie.
Her voice sounded odd inside the tunnel walls.
"I want to go back. I don't like it," said Phyllis.
"I don't care what you say, I won't keep walking in the dark."
"Don't be silly, Phyllis," Peter said.
"I've got half of a candle and some matches."
He listened for a second. "What's that?"
There was a low, humming noise on the railway line.
The sound grew louder and louder.
"It's a train," said Bobbie.
"Let me go back,"
cried Phyllis, struggling to get away from Bobbie's hand.
"Don't be scared.
It's quite safe," said Bobbie. "Stand back."
"Come up here!
There's a space!" Peter shouted.
The sound of the train was now a roar.
Bobbie dragged Phyllis farther into the tunnel, toward Peter's voice.
There was a small space dug out of the tunnel wall.
They stood there while the train roared louder and louder.
It seemed as if it would deafen them.
In the distance they could see the lights of the train.
They were like a dragon's eyes.
The train was screaming toward them.
Phyllis and Bobbie clung to each other.
The train roared by, light flashing from its windows.
The children felt a blast of hot air and smelled smoke.
Even Peter grabbed Bobbie's arm.
Later he explained that it was "in case she was scared." Slowly
the noise got softer and the lights got smaller and smaller and smaller. With
one last whee ! the train left the tunnel.
"Oh!" said the children together, in a whisper.
Peter lit the candle with a shaking hand.
"Come on," he said, his voice shaking too.
"Oh!" said Phyllis.
"What if the boy with the red shirt was in the way of the train?"
"We must keep looking for him," said Peter.
They went on into the deeper darkness of the tunnel.
Peter went first, holding the candle to light the way.
Suddenly Peter stood still and shouted, "Hello!"
Then he hurried ahead.
When the girls reached him, they saw the boy.
Peter had stopped about a meter from him.
Phyllis saw something red and shut her eyes tight.
The boy in the red shirt was on the ground, beside the tracks.
His eyes were closed, and he did not move.
"Is he . . . dead?" asked Phyllis, still closing her eyes.
"Dead? No!" said Peter. "He's fainted, that's all.
What should we do?"
"Can we move him?" asked Bobbie.
"I don't know, he's a big fellow," replied Peter.
"How about we put some water on his forehead?"
"We don't have any water, but we have some milk from lunch," Bobbie said.
"Let's try that!"
"Yes, and I think people sometimes rub people's hands to help them wake up," said Phyllis.
So Bobbie splashed warm milk onto his forehead while Peter rubbed the boy's hands.
Then together the three children said, "Please wake up! Please speak!"
"Open your eyes! Speak to us! Please!"
The children said these words over and over again to the boy in the red shirt.
"Wet his ears with milk," Bobbie suggested.
"When people faint, they use perfume.
I think milk is just as good."
So they wet his ears with milk.
It was very dark in the tunnel.
Peter's candle was now really short, and not very bright.
"Oh, please open your eyes!" moaned Phyllis.
"I believe he's dead."
"He isn't," insisted Bobbie.
Peter shook the boy's arm.
Slowly the boy opened his eyes and sighed quietly.
"Oh, he's not dead," cried Phyllis. "I knew he wasn't."
She began to cry.
"What's the matter?
I'm all right," said the boy.
"Phyllis, please be quiet," Peter said. "Drink this."
"What is it?" the boy asked.
"It's milk," said Peter. "Don't worry, we will help you."
So the boy drank and the children were quiet.
"He'll be fine after the milk," Peter whispered to his sisters.
"I'm better now," the boy announced.
He tried to move but started to groan.
"I . . . I . . . think I've broken my leg," he said slowly.
"Did you fall over?" asked Phyllis.
"I tripped on a wire," the boy explained.
"I couldn't stand, so I sat down.
It does hurt, though.
How did you all get here?"
"We saw all the boys go into the tunnel," Bobbie began.
"And we saw everyone come out of the tunnel—but not you.
So we came to rescue you," Peter finished proudly.
"You're all brave, that's for sure!" said the boy.
"Oh, it's nothing," said Peter.
"Can you walk if we help you?"
"I can try," said the boy.
He tried, but he could only stand on one foot.
"Oh, I must sit down, it hurts too much."
He sat down again and went to sleep.
The children looked at each other.
"Go and get help," said Bobbie. "I'll stay with him."
Peter looked worried.
"Let me stay, and you and Phyllis go."
"No, you and Phyllis go," Bobbie said.
"Lend me your knife and I'll cut his boot before he wakes up.
Just be quick!"
Bobbie watched them disappear and put the little candle on the ground.
"Now don't be a silly little girl!" she said to herself.
Bobbie was always very angry if anybody called her a "silly little girl."
But when she was angry with herself, she could say it.
Then she opened Peter's knife and used it to cut the boy's boot.
Bobbie tried to pull off his sock, but his leg was too swollen.
It seemed the tunnel was getting darker.
Nothing seemed quite real.
"Silly little girl," Bobbie said again.
She looked at his broken leg.
"It needs something soft under it," she thought.
Then she remembered her petticoat.
She took it off and carefully put it under the boy's leg.
There was nothing else to do but wait.
Bobbie waited with the boy in the dark tunnel.
The candle was almost out.
Finally the boy woke up.
"Oh! I'm glad you woke up," said Bobbie.
"Please don't faint again!
What's your name?"
"Jim," he said.
"My name's Bobbie," she said.
"But you're a girl, aren't you?" he asked.
"Yes, my real name is Roberta.
I wish I were a boy, though," said Bobbie.
"My brother and sister went to get help."
"Why didn't you go with them?" Jim asked.
"Someone had to stay with you," Bobbie said.
"Well, Bobbie, you're very brave!" said Jim.
"The candle is out," said Bobbie.
"Are you afraid of the dark, Bobbie?" asked Jim.
"No, not very afraid," said Bobbie. "But . . ."
"Let's hold hands," said Jim kindly.
He put his big hand over her small hand.
They sat and waited.
Meanwhile Peter and Phyllis ran to a farm to get help.
When the two children arrived with some farmers, they found Bobbie and Jim asleep.
The farmers carried Jim on a plank of wood.
"Where does he live?" asked a farmer.
"In Northumberland," answered Bobbie.
"He told me while we were waiting.
Bring him to our house first.
It's not far along the road.
I'm sure Mother will say it's all right."
Mother did say it was all right, although she was surprised.
"I'm sorry to be so much trouble,"
Jim said to Mother as the men carried him in.
His face was still white with pain.
"Don't worry, dear, the doctor will come soon."
Mother also sent a message to Jim's school to tell them what had happened.
"My grandfather lives near here," said Jim.
"I'll write and tell him," said Mother.
The next day someone knocked at the front door.
"That'll be the doctor again," said Mother.
But it wasn't the doctor.
The children recognized the visitor's voice.
But who was it?
Then Mother called out, "Jim's grandfather has come.
He wants to see you all."
They followed Mother into the front room, and there was . . . the old gentleman!
"Oh, it's you!" cried Bobbie.
The children were excited to see him.
"But you're not going to take Jim away, are you?
I was hoping he could stay for a while," Peter said.
The old gentleman smiled. "No," he said.
"Your mother is very kind.
Jim will stay here and she'll look after him."
"What about Mother's writing?"
Peter said, before anyone could stop him.
The old gentleman smiled kindly at Mother.
"She can stop writing, and there will be enough food," he said.
"Bobbie," said the old man, "can you show me to the door?"
The old gentleman and Bobbie walked outside.
"I received your letter, Bobbie, but it wasn't necessary.
I had already read the newspaper.
I tried to help him.
I haven't done much, but I have hope."
"Oh!" said Bobbie, crying a little.
"But keep your secret a little longer," he said.
"You don't think Father did it, do you?" said Bobbie.
"I'm sure he didn't," said the old gentleman.
Life at home was better with Jim around.
He told the children stories about his school.
Now that Mother was not writing stories every day, she gave the children some lessons.
"I wonder if the railway misses us," said Phyllis.
"We haven't waved to the 9:15 in a long time.
Let's do it tomorrow!"
So the next morning they ran down to the fence.
They watched the 9:15 train coming out of the tunnel.
"Take our love to Father!"
they shouted as they waved their handkerchiefs.
The old gentleman waved from his window.
And there was nothing strange about that, because he had always waved.
But something was different.
People waved handkerchiefs and newspapers from every window of the train.
Their smiling faces looked at the children.
"Well!" said the children. "Why did everybody wave?"
"Perhaps the old gentleman asked the people to wave," said Bobbie.
And that was just what had happened!
The old gentleman had gotten to his station early, and he had talked to every passenger.
Some passengers were surprised.
Some were curious while others were doubtful or grumpy.
But then the passengers sat inside the train and read a particular story in the newspaper.
That made them all very pleased.
Later, when they saw the children, they all waved.
Back at home later, Bobbie could not concentrate at all.
Mother excused her from the morning lessons.
"I'll go and talk to Perks at the station," thought Bobbie.
At the station it seemed as if everyone was holding a newspaper.
Several people smiled at Bobbie as she went by—people who never usually smiled at her.
"How strange," she thought.
Perks wasn't anywhere so Bobbie chatted with the station cat.
"How friendly everyone is today," she remarked.
Perks appeared when it was time for the 11:54 to arrive.
He had a newspaper too.
"Hello!" he said to Bobbie.
"I saw it in the newspaper, and I'm so happy for you!"
"What did you see in the newspaper?" asked Bobbie.
But already the 11:54 was steaming into the station.
Perks looked in all the train windows.
Only three people got off the train.
The first was a woman with three boxes.
The second was a woman with a brown suitcase.
And the third . . .
"Oh! My daddy, my daddy!" cried Bobbie.
People put their heads out of the windows.
Everyone looked at the tall, pale man and the little girl who was hugging him.
Bobbie thought she could never let go.
"Didn't Mother get my letter this morning?" asked Father.
"There wasn't any mail this morning," Bobbie said.
"Oh, Daddy, is it really you?"
Father held her hand and said, "It's all right.
They caught the real spy."
"Everybody knows that you aren't a spy," said Bobbie proudly.
"We—me, Mother, and the old gentleman—always knew that."
"Yes, I must thank your friend," said Father.
Father and Bobbie walked together to the house.
Bobbie rushed inside first, trying to think of a way to tell Mother the news.
Father waited in the garden, looking at all the flowers.
He had been locked away for so long, each one seemed like a tiny miracle now.
A second later Bobbie threw open the door.
"Come in, Daddy," she shouted. "Come home!"
